# Concept library

<!-- Generated by `bun run scripts/concepts-index.ts` from `src/concepts/library.ts`. Do not edit by hand. -->

The 66 economic ideas that Iceland Inc. can show as "at play" when you click a flow, a player or an indicator. Rules, terms, flows, levers and indicators refer to them by id. Each entry in `src/concepts/library.ts` also has a plain-English explanation, references and related ideas.

## Accounting

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `double-entry` | Double-entry bookkeeping | Every payment is recorded twice, as a minus for the payer and a plus for the payee, so money never appears or vanishes unnoticed. | accounting |
| `stock-flow-consistency` | Stock-flow consistency | Stocks such as deposits and debts change only because flows add to or subtract from them, and every financial asset is someone's liability. | accounting |
| `net-worth` | Net worth | What a player owns minus what it owes. It grows with saving and revaluations, not with borrowing. | accounting |
| `sectoral-balances` | Sectoral balances | The surpluses and deficits of the private sector, the government and the rest of the world always sum to zero. | accounting |
| `accrual-vs-cash` | Accrual versus cash | Some income is earned without any money changing hands, such as indexation added to a loan. Accounts record it when it is earned. | accounting |
| `revaluation` | Revaluation | A change in the price of something already owned, such as foreign shares when the króna falls. It changes wealth without any payment. | accounting |
| `haig-simons-income` | Income after inflation (Haig–Simons income) | What you could spend while keeping your wealth intact. Inflation eats savings, so part of the interest on them is not really income. | accounting |

## Money

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `endogenous-money` | Endogenous money: loans create deposits | When a bank lends, it creates a new deposit for the borrower. Most money is created this way, not printed by the central bank. | post-keynesian |
| `money-destruction` | Money destruction: repayment destroys deposits | When a borrower repays a bank loan, the deposit used to pay is cancelled along with the debt, and the money stock shrinks. | accounting |
| `reserves-and-payments` | Reserves and the payment system | Banks settle payments with each other, and with the government, in reserves: accounts they hold at the central bank. | institutional |
| `deficits-and-money` | Government deficits and money | Deficits add deposits when banks or the central bank buy the bonds, and move existing money when pension funds or savers buy them. | accounting |
| `broad-money` | Broad money (M3) | Notes, coins and bank deposits held by the public. In Iceland almost all of it is bank deposits. | institutional |

## Credit

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `credit-impulse` | Credit impulse | The change in the flow of new borrowing. A steady credit flow means zero impulse; only speeding up or slowing down moves demand growth. | post-keynesian |
| `debt-service-constraint` | Debt-service constraint | Iceland caps new mortgage payments at 35% of disposable income (40% for first-time buyers), tested at stressed interest rates and terms. | institutional |
| `loan-to-value` | Loan-to-value cap | A limit on the size of a mortgage relative to the home's value: in Iceland 80%, or 90% for first-time buyers. | institutional |
| `amortisation` | Amortisation | Paying off a loan's principal over time. Annuity loans have level payments; equal-principal loans start high and fall. | institutional |
| `indexation` | CPI indexation | Icelandic indexed loans add inflation to the principal each month. National accounts treat that as interest earned, not as a price change. | institutional |
| `interest-distribution` | Interest as distribution | Every debt carries an interest flow from debtor to creditor. Higher rates move income from borrowers to savers, often before they reduce spending. | post-keynesian |
| `bank-capital` | Bank capital and the limits to money creation | Banks can create money by lending, but profitability, borrowers' demand and capital rules limit how far and how fast. | institutional |
| `minsky-instability` | Minsky's financial instability hypothesis | Long periods of stability encourage riskier borrowing, so a financial system can drift from safe to fragile on its own. | post-keynesian |

## Prices and wages

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `markup-pricing` | Markup pricing | Firms set prices by adding a margin to their cost per unit, above all wages and imported inputs. | post-keynesian |
| `cost-pass-through` | Cost pass-through | How much, and how fast, higher costs such as wages show up in the prices firms charge. | empirical |
| `exchange-rate-pass-through` | Exchange-rate pass-through | When the króna falls, imports cost more in krónur. Pass-through measures how much of that reaches consumer prices, and how fast. | empirical |
| `wage-bargaining` | Wage bargaining in Iceland | Collective agreements cover about 90% of Icelandic workers or more, with pattern-setting private deals and inflation review clauses. | institutional |
| `wage-phillips-curve` | Wage Phillips curve | Wages tend to rise faster when unemployment is low and more slowly when it is high. | keynesian |
| `reservation-wage` | Reservation wage | The lowest pay a job-seeker will accept. More generous unemployment benefits raise it, so people search longer and pay demands firm up. | new-keynesian |
| `adaptive-expectations` | Adaptive expectations | People expect future inflation to look like recent inflation, revising their forecast gradually as prices surprise them. | monetarist |
| `anchored-expectations` | Anchored expectations | When people trust the inflation target, they expect inflation to return to it, so shocks fade instead of feeding on themselves. | new-keynesian |
| `profit-squeeze` | Profit squeeze | Profits are what is left after costs, so a pay rise not matched by prices cuts profits proportionally more than wages rise. | post-keynesian |
| `real-wages` | Real wages | What a wage can buy: pay adjusted for prices. Real wages rise only when pay grows faster than inflation. | keynesian |

## Demand and output

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `consumption-function` | Consumption function | Household spending depends mainly on income, and also on wealth, interest rates, new borrowing and fear of unemployment. | keynesian |
| `paradox-of-thrift` | Paradox of thrift | If everyone tries to save more at once, spending and incomes fall, and total saving may not rise at all. | keynesian |
| `multiplier` | The multiplier | An extra króna of spending becomes someone's income, part of which is spent again, so the total effect can exceed the first injection. | keynesian |
| `investment-accelerator` | Investment accelerator | Firms invest more when sales are growing and they need more capacity, so investment swings harder than output. | keynesian |
| `import-leakage` | Import leakage | Part of every króna spent in Iceland buys imports, so it supports incomes abroad and leaks out of the domestic income circuit. | keynesian |
| `capacity-utilisation` | Capacity utilisation | How hard firms are running their existing staff and equipment. High utilisation means pressure on prices; low utilisation means slack. | post-keynesian |
| `okun-law` | Okun's law | When output grows more slowly than its trend, unemployment tends to rise, by a roughly stable amount per point of lost output. | empirical |
| `habit-persistence` | Habit persistence | People adjust spending gradually because they are used to a standard of living, so consumption responds slowly to changes in income. | new-keynesian |
| `migration-buffer` | Migration as a buffer | Foreign workers come to Iceland when jobs are plentiful and fewer come when jobs are scarce, softening swings in unemployment. | empirical |

## Policy

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `taylor-rule` | Taylor rule | A simple recipe for setting interest rates: raise them when inflation is above target or the economy runs hot, cut them when below. | new-keynesian |
| `interest-rate-channel` | Interest-rate channel | How a change in the key rate reaches spending: through the rates banks and the government pay and charge, saving and borrowing. | keynesian |
| `policy-lags` | Policy lags | Interest-rate changes take many months, often more than a year, to have their largest effect on output and inflation. | monetarist |
| `automatic-stabilisers` | Automatic stabilisers | Taxes that fall and benefits that rise in a downturn cushion incomes without any new decision by the government. | keynesian |
| `fiscal-rule` | Iceland's fiscal stability rule | Since 2026, the state's underlying spending may grow by at most 2% a year in real terms, with some items outside the cap. | institutional |
| `debt-feedback` | Debt-tied tax rule (fiscal reaction function) | Taxes rise when government debt is above its anchor and fall when it is below, so debt cannot drift away for good. | institutional |
| `macroprudential-policy` | Macroprudential policy | Rules that protect the financial system as a whole, such as caps on mortgage borrowing and extra capital buffers for banks. | institutional |
| `bond-buyers` | Who buys government bonds | Whether banks, the central bank, pension funds or foreigners buy new government bonds changes the money supply, who earns the interest and the króna. | institutional |

## External

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `floating-exchange-rate` | Floating exchange rate | The króna's value is set each day by supply of and demand for krónur, not fixed by the central bank. | institutional |
| `carry-trade` | Carry trade | Investors borrow in low-interest currencies to hold high-interest ones, such as the króna, pushing it up until the trade unwinds. | empirical |
| `current-account` | Current account | Iceland's income from the rest of the world minus its payments to it: trade, plus cross-border interest, dividends and transfers. | accounting |
| `real-exchange-rate` | Real exchange rate | The exchange rate adjusted for prices or wages at home and abroad: a measure of how competitive Icelandic goods and services are. | empirical |
| `purchasing-power-parity` | Purchasing power parity | The idea that, in the long run, exchange rates should make the same goods cost the same everywhere. | empirical |
| `export-sectors` | Iceland's export sectors | Tourism, marine products, aluminium and, increasingly, intellectual property earn most of Iceland's foreign currency. | empirical |
| `terms-of-trade` | Terms of trade | The price of what Iceland sells abroad compared with the price of what it buys. When fish or aluminium prices rise, Iceland is richer. | empirical |
| `dutch-disease` | Dutch disease | A boom in one export lifts wages and the currency, which makes other exports, such as tourism, less competitive. | empirical |
| `resource-rent` | Resource rent | Profit from a natural resource beyond what it takes to keep producing, such as the value of fishing quotas or of cheap hydropower. | institutional |

## Housing

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `credit-and-house-prices` | Mortgage credit and house prices | Rising house prices need a growing flow of mortgage money, so price growth tends to follow the acceleration of mortgage credit. | post-keynesian |
| `housing-wealth-effect` | Housing wealth effect | When home values rise, owners feel richer and can borrow more against their homes, so they tend to spend a little more. | empirical |

## Pensions

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `funded-pensions` | Iceland's funded pensions | Workers and employers pay at least 15.5% of wages into pension funds, whose assets are worth about 180% of GDP. | institutional |
| `pension-entitlements` | Pension entitlements | Households' claims on pension funds count as household wealth in the national accounts, and as liabilities of the funds. | accounting |

## Distribution

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `borrowers-and-savers` | Borrowers and savers | The same shock helps some households and hurts others, depending on whether they owe money or own it. | empirical |
| `intergenerational-flows` | Flows between generations | Young households borrow to buy homes from older ones, so rate rises and inflation move income and wealth between generations. | empirical |

## Modelling

| Id | Title | One-liner | School |
|---|---|---|---|
| `steady-state-baseline` | Steady-state baseline | Iceland Inc. starts from a calm economy in which every ratio holds still, so the effect of a single change can be seen clearly. | post-keynesian |
| `counterfactual` | Counterfactuals | To measure what a change did, compare the shocked run with an unshocked run of the same model, not with the past. | empirical |
| `model-limits` | What this model can and cannot tell you | Iceland Inc. is a teaching simplification that shows mechanisms and orders of magnitude. It is not a forecast. | empirical |
| `gradual-adjustment` | Gradual adjustment | People and firms close the gap between where they are and where they want to be step by step, not all at once. | post-keynesian |
